title: Security Best Practices
subtitle: Non-root users, read-only filesystems, minimal images, and secret management

content.text: By default, processes inside Docker containers run as root. If your application has a vulnerability that lets an attacker execute code inside the container, root access inside means they can potentially escape the container, read other containers' data, or mount the host filesystem. Container security is about reducing the blast radius of a breach through multiple layers of defense.

content.code:
FROM node:20-alpine

# Create a non-root user and group
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .

# Give ownership of /app to appuser BEFORE switching
RUN chown -R appuser:appgroup /app

# Switch to non-root user — all subsequent commands and the running container
# will use this user
USER appuser

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# Verify: docker run --rm myapp whoami → 'appuser' (not root)

# Larger images = more packages = more CVEs to patch

# Scan images for vulnerabilities:
docker scout cves node:20           # Docker's built-in scanner
docker scout cves node:20-slim
docker scout cves node:20-alpine
# alpine typically has 10-20x fewer CVEs than the full Debian image

# Distroless images (Google): no shell, no package manager
# Even harder to exploit — no /bin/bash for an attacker to use
# FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12

# Good → Better → Best:
# node:20 → node:20-slim → node:20-alpine → distroless

# Regularly update base images
docker pull node:20-alpine   # get latest patches
docker build --no-cache -t myapp .  # rebuild without cache

docker run \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp \
  --tmpfs /app/logs \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --user 1001:1001 \
  myapp

# --read-only: the container filesystem is read-only
#              attackers can't write malware, change configs, etc.
# --tmpfs /tmp: writable temp dir in memory (since we're read-only)
# --cap-drop ALL: drop ALL Linux capabilities
# --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE: re-add ONLY what's needed (bind ports <1024)
# --security-opt no-new-privileges: process can't escalate privileges
# --user 1001:1001: run as a non-root UID

content.filename: Secret hygiene — avoid leaking secrets in layers
content.code:
# ❌ WRONG — secret baked into image layer (visible in docker history)
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
RUN npm config set registry https://user:TOKEN@registry.npmjs.org

# ❌ WRONG — even if you delete in next layer, it's in the history
RUN curl -H 'Authorization: Token $API_KEY' ...
RUN unset API_KEY  # too late — it's in the previous layer

# ✅ RIGHT — use BuildKit secrets (never stored in layers)
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.4
FROM node:20-alpine
# --mount=type=secret mounts the secret file only during this RUN step
# and it is NOT stored in the image layer
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) \
    npm config set //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN && \
    npm install && \
    npm config delete //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken

# Build with:
docker build --secret id=npm_token,src=.npm-token -t myapp .

questions.question: You accidentally add a secret API key in a RUN command, then delete it in the next RUN. Is the key still in the image?
options: No — the delete command removes it from all layers
Yes — each RUN creates a new layer; the key is in the first layer and 'docker history' can reveal it
Only if you push the image to a public registry
No — Docker automatically redacts secrets from history
questions.explanation: Layers are immutable. Even if you 'unset' or 'rm' a secret in a later RUN, the secret exists in the earlier layer and can be extracted with 'docker history' or by exporting the image as a tar and inspecting the layers. Always use BuildKit's --mount=type=secret or pass secrets only at runtime with -e, never during build.

faq.q: How do I scan my images for known vulnerabilities?
faq.a: Several options: (1) 'docker scout cves <image>' — built into Docker Desktop; (2) Trivy (aquasecurity/trivy) — free, fast, widely used: 'trivy image myapp:latest'; (3) Snyk — integrates with GitHub and CI. Make scanning part of your CI pipeline so new vulnerabilities in base images are caught before deployment.

examples: Kubernetes Pod Security Standards mandate non-root containers and read-only root filesystems by default in restricted mode — learning these practices now prepares you for K8s
GitHub's own production containers run as non-root with all capabilities dropped — it's a baseline expectation in modern security-conscious engineering teams
